lines.watchItem: Demand behind leading-edge wafer starts is still climbing: the four biggest cloud buyers guide to roughly $725 billion of 2026 spending and one bank sees about $4.1 trillion over 2026 to 2028. TSMC has already lifted its own 2026 growth and spending plans on the back of it.

Stacked memory, not wafers, is what caps finished accelerators right now: suppliers can cover only 60 to 70 percent of what NVIDIA asked for, and one maker says customers want about half again more than it can promise. Wafer orders can therefore run ahead of what memory lets customers actually ship.

Advanced-packaging lines stay the tightest link in the chain, booked through 2027 even as monthly capacity heads toward 130,000 to 140,000 wafers. Reports disagree on whether the shortfall has narrowed to about 10 percent or is still near 20 percent, so how tight allocation really is remains an open question.

Packaging capacity is pre-booked by very few names: the top three hold more than 85 percent and NVIDIA alone about 60 percent. That leaves the packaging book exposed to a single buyer changing its plans, and both merchant vendors carry the same concentration in their own order books.

The leading-node customer list is broadening away from the two merchant GPU makers: Microsoft is negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 in-house accelerators for 2027, Google has widened its custom-chip suppliers, and a model builder is in early talks to use a rival 2nm line. Custom chips are forecast to grow far faster than merchant GPUs this year.

Pricing power sits with whoever is scarcest. The leading GPU vendor holds a 75 percent gross margin and is reported to be lifting AI system prices more than 15 percent for early-next-year shipments as memory contract prices run up about 50 percent this year, while TSMC's own gross margin reached 67.7 percent.

Second sources are stirring on both packaging and wafers: Google has committed to more than 3 million units of Intel bridge packaging for a 2028 part, that process is claimed at roughly half the cost of CoWoS, Samsung raised contract chipmaking prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders, and Intel's foundry revenue grew 31 percent. These are the events that could move where AI packaging and wafer work is placed.

Policy keeps a slice of end demand off the table and is getting more forceful: Taiwan prosecutors indicted nine people over diverted AI servers, Beijing told licensed buyers to keep the hardware in Hong Kong, and the leading vendor's China revenue halved year on year. Any wafer or packaging volume tied to China-bound parts carries that exposure.
